notes.body: assigned to @martin.r.mathieson
changed title from Try to check valid encoding values against item type to Try to check for valid encoding values against item type
mentioned in merge request !19715
Not sure if UUID is endianness sensitive.

README.dissector says:

For integral, floating-point, Boolean, FT_GUID, and FT_EUI64 fields,
the encoding specifies the byte order of the value; the 'encoding'
argument should be ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN if the value is little-endian
and ENC_BIG_ENDIAN if it is big-endian.

And proto.c:2965 has

proto_tree_set_guid_tvb(new_fi, tvb, start, encoding);

tvb_get_guid does use the encoding value.

Yes, the endianness matters.

Microsoft GUIDs are basically mixed endian, they're treated as a struct consisting of several little endian integer components plus an array that usually has an EUI-48 and is thus in network byte order. (Though compare Raymond Chen vs. Raymond Chen https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20190426-00/?p=102450 https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20220928-00/?p=107221)

Bluetooth UUIDs are little endian in the sense that the entire 16 bytes are transmitted in the other order. Right now those are all actually treated with some custom stuff in the Bluetooth dissectors and often FT_BYTES, but probably should be a field type compatible with FT_GUID.

There are others, like above, that should just be treated as big endian.

This is mostly significant for the string representation and sorting.

UUIDs?  It's. Complicated.

There are a bunch of different formats.

The 4-bit "variant" field, described in [section 4.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562#section-4.1) of [RFC 9562](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562), is the place to start when determining the format. See [the "Variants" subsection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier#Variants) of [the "Format" section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier#Format) of [the Wikipedia article on UUIDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier).

If the variant field has a bit value of the form `0xxx`, it's the Apollo NCS variant, "variant 0". According to [the "NCS (variant 0) UUID" section](https://misc.daniel-marschall.de/tools/uuid_mac_decoder/#gen_uuid_ncs) of [this page](https://misc.daniel-marschall.de/tools/uuid_mac_decoder/), the time stamp field in that format hit its maximum at some point on 2015-09-05, so it's not being generated any more, but *maybe* you'll see some on the wire with UUIDs generated a while ago.  That UUID has a 48-bit time stamp, a 16-bit reserved field, a one-bit field that's always zero (which corresponds to the `0` in the variant field), a 7-bit address family field, and a 56-bit "node" field, which presumably contains an address in that address family. The last possible UUID for a host whose "node" ID is the loopback IP address 127.0.0.1 is `ffffffff-ffff-0000-027f-000001000000`, [which is interpreted like this](https://misc.daniel-marschall.de/tools/uuid_mac_decoder/interpret_uuid.php?uuid=ffffffff-ffff-0000-027f-000001000000).  According to [this issue comment](https://github.com/ietf-wg-uuidrev/rfc4122bis/issues/144#issuecomment-1712337364), the address family values look like somebody's (Apollo Computing's, to be precise) idea of an `AF_` value, given that "unspecified" is 0 (`AF_UNSPEC`/`socket_$unspec`), "unix" is 1 (`AF_UNIX`/`socket_$unix`), "internet" is 2 (`AF_INET`/`socket_$internet`), and so on. However, 4.2 BSD's assignments stopped at 11 being `AF_SNA`, so it's not obvious what `socket_$unspec2` or `socket_$dds` were - and apparently only 0, 2, and 13 were used. From section 3.1.3 "Configuring a Global Broker in Networks with Apollo Systems" of [the Ultrix "Guide to the [DCE] Location Broker" manual](http://www.bitsavers.org/pdf/dec/vax/ultrix-32/4.0_Jun90/AA-PBKSA-TE_ULTRIX_Guide_to_the_Location_Broker_Jun90.pdf) (DCE having been derived from Apollo NCS), it appears that "DDS" refers to Apollo's own Domain network communications protocols originally developed for their proprietary token ring network.

The fields other than the time stamp are probably just octet sequences, so they have no endianness. I think the time stamp is big-endian, given that Apollo used big-endian 68k processors when they started out.

So the first step in parsing a UUID is to look at the uppermost bit of octet 8 of the UUID and, if it's 0, parse it as an Apollo NCS UUID.

Otherwise, if it's 1, parse it as a UUID in which the upper 4 bits of octet 8 are the variant field.

Variants 8 through 11 are parsed as per RFC 9562. They have a "version" field, described in [section 4.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562#section-4.2) of [RFC 9562](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562). See [the "Variants" subsection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier#Variants) of [the "Format" section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier#Format) of [the Wikipedia article on UUIDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier).

Variants 12 and 13 are reserved for "Microsoft Corporation backward compatibility". See, I guess, Raymond Chen's two postings, the second of which is cited by RFC 9562.

Variant 14 and 15 are reserved for future use.

So, at least for the OSF DCE/RFC formats, and, I guess, the old Apollo NCF format, *individual subfields* are in known byte orders; *maybe* that's the case for the Microsoft COM formats.

But it sounds as if Bluetooth, for whatever reason, may put the 16 octets of *the UUID as a whole* onto the wire in reverse order. Presumably *that's* what the encoding of a UUID/GUID should specify - `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` for normal and `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN` for Bluetooth *if* they use RFC 9562 format and then transmit uuid[15], uuid[14], uuid[13], ..., uuid[2], uuid[1], uuid[0].

> But it sounds as if Bluetooth, for whatever reason, may put the 16 octets of the UUID as a whole onto the wire in reverse order

Yes, that's what it does. Though currently all the Bluetooth UUIDs are handled as FT_BYTES fields and byte reversed by functions in the Bluetooth dissectors. Bluetooth also has a convention whereby a UUID can be given with just two (or hypothetically four bytes, but none yet assigned), in which case the other bytes are assumed to be filled in by 0000XXXX-0000-1000-8000-00805F9B34FB, a base UUID used by the Bluetooth SIG. These 16 bit UUIDs are registered with the Bluetooth SIG.

Given that, if Bluetooth UUIDs were to be handled as a UUID like field type, it might be useful to have special handling for 16 bit and 32 bit literals / packet length, which might mean having a separate FT_BT_UUID which is compatible but not the same as the other FT_GUID. In which case maybe it's ok to have the FT_GUID still to have the ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN mean the Microsoft "the individual subfields are little endian." But maybe that isn't necessary if Little Endian subfields are always indicated by the variant type and Microsoft always uses types 12 and 13.

> Bluetooth also has a convention whereby a UUID can be given with just two (or hypothetically four bytes, but none yet assigned), in which case the other bytes are assumed to be filled in by 0000XXXX-0000-1000-8000-00805F9B34FB, a base UUID used by the Bluetooth SIG.

So that sounds like an `ENC_UUID_BT_2_OCTET` encoding for a 2-octet field (and possibly an `ENC_UUID_BT_4_OCTET` encoding for a 4-octet field if they're assigned); they'd normally be combined with `ENC_LITLE_ENDIAN`, but if there's ever a case where the two octets in question are sent in big-endian order, they could be combined with `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN`. There'd also be `ENC_UUID_RFC_9562`, which handles all the encodings they mention (including ones where they say "see something else`, i.e. Apollo NCF and Microsoft-compatibiity), and the "reserved for future use" ones), and that'd have `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` for the normal case and `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN` for the Bluetooth case.

> In which case maybe it's ok to have the FT_GUID still to have the ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN mean the Microsoft "the individual subfields are little endian." But maybe that isn't necessary if Little Endian subfields are always indicated by the variant type and Microsoft always uses types 12 and 13.

[RFC 9562 section 4 "UUID Format"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562#name-uuid-format) says that  all fields are big-endian, at least for the formats discussed there. However, I'm guessing that fields such as `node_id` are just octet strings put out in "start with the first octet" form.  The *primary* place where that matters is probably the timestamp; RFC 9562 indicates, in [section 2.1 "Update Motivation"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562#name-update-motivation), that one goal for the RFC was to have formats where sorting by time stamp, for formats using a time stamp, is easier.

In *most* of the versions of the OSF DCE/IETF RFC 9562 variant, the time stamp is mixed-endian, with each individual piece being big-endian but the pieces themselves being sent lowest-order piece first. It appears that, in the Microsoft-compatibility variants, the time stamp is little-endian, with a little-endian order of little-endian pieces.

I think that only Microsoft uses the Microsoft-compatibility variants. They may well use *other* variants as well, presumably with mixed-endian or big-endian time stamps for the OSF DCE/IETF RFC 9562 variant with versions that have time stamps.

I don't propose to fix FT_GUID in this change.  Out of the calls my script can detect, we have:
- ENC_BIG_ENDIAN (98)
- ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN (59)
- ENC_NA (16)

I guess those 16 NA cases can probably be changed to ENC_BIG_ENDIAN for now/soon.
Not sure of Ethertype is endianness sensitive.
FT_ETHER isn't, but this is a 2-byte enum field..
...and is, in fact, big-endian in most if not all places, so this change is correct.

Bluetooth also sends EUI-48 in Little Endian order, which is why packet-bluetooth has a `dissect_bd_addr` function that retrieves the bytes in opposite order and then calls `proto_tree_add_ether` with the value after byte swapping. Several Bluetooth dissectors call that. So perhap FT_ETHER should support ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN.

I could in future allow ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN in the script for FT_ETHER, but note that in README:dissector:1500 it still says that the encoding arg should be ENC_NA

Note that all of the calls that my script can see, presently call FT_ETHER items with ENC_NA.

MAC-48/EUI-48 and EUI-64 addresses aren't numerical quantities - and, unlike numerical quantities, where if the endianness matches the host endianness, a memory fetch will, if the data is aligned such that it can be loaded as an operand, fetch the data in an appropriate family for the host -  so I'm not sure big-endian is the correct name for the "usual" byte order or that little-endian is the correct name for the "other" byte order.

To quote IEEE standard 802-2014, section 8 "MAC addresses", subsection 8.1 "Terms and notational conventions"

> Hexadecimal representation is a sequence of octet values in which the values of the individual octets are displayed in order from left to right, with each octet value represented as a 2-digit hexadecimal numeral and with the resulting pairs of hexadecimal digits separated by hyphens. The order of the hexadecimal digits in each pair, as well as the mapping between the hexadecimal digits and the bits of the octet value, is derived by interpreting the bits of the octet value as a binary numeral using the normal mathematical rules for digit significance.

Where in the Bluetooth pecification does it indicate the byte order in which a [BD_ADDR](https://www.bluetooth.com/wp-content/uploads/Files/Specification/HTML/Core-60/out/en/br-edr-controller/baseband-specification.html#UUID-550112f9-4948-6a09-ea08-884dae09b6bc) is sent out on the wire, and what terminology do they use?

From the Core specification, Low Energy Controller (Vol. 6) Part B [there's this:](https://www.bluetooth.com/wp-content/uploads/Files/Specification/HTML/Core-54/out/en/low-energy-controller/link-layer-specification.html#UUID-90a5a1bb-d4f6-76e6-7f9a-f6e126d4499d)

> Multi-octet fields, with the exception of the Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) and the Message Integrity Check (MIC), shall be transmitted with the least significant octet first. Each octet within multi-octet fields, with the exception of the CRC (see Section 3.1.1), shall be transmitted in LSB first order. **For example, the 48-bit addresses in the advertising physical channel PDUs shall be transmitted with the least significant octet first, followed by the remainder of the five octets in increasing order.**

Plus the diagrams there and [also here](https://www.bluetooth.com/wp-content/uploads/Files/Specification/HTML/Core-54/out/en/br-edr-controller/baseband-specification.html#UUID-1ff70a45-fdcc-31c1-d467-cabf78823423)

So was it the IEEE or the Bluetooth SIG that introduced the notion that the octets of a MAC-48/EUI-48 or an EUI-64 have numerical significance to the extent that a MAC/EUI field can have a "byte order" in the big-endian/little-endian sense? I'm not seeing anything obvious in IEEE standard 802-2014; they speak of the significance of the bits within each octet, but I'm not seeing where they assign numerical significance to the octets.

I'm tempted to have have `ENC_NORMAL` and `ENC_BYTE_SWAPPED` for this case, with `ENC_NORMAL` == `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` and `ENC_BYTE_SWAPPED` == `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, unless some *non*-Bluetooth source has assigned numerical significance to octets in MAC/EUI values.

And the DIX 2.0 Ethernet specification, which I think was the source from which the IEEE 48-bit address concept was derived, says that:

> The first bit of a data link address distinguishes physical from multicast addresses:
> 
> 0 => physical address
> 1 => multicast address
> 
> In either case, the remainder of the first octet and all of the subsequent octets form a 47-bit pattern.

The spec also says

> With the exception of Section 8, this document does not define an order of transmission for the octets of standard multi-octet data types (strings,integers, etc.), since no values of such data types appear in the data link frame format. The order in which implementations of the Ethernet store the octets of a frame in computer memory, and the manner in which higher level protocols interpret the contents of the data field as values of various multi-octet data types, are beyond the scope of this specification.

Section 8 "Ethernet Configuration Testing Protocol" describes a protocol running *atop* Ethernet, with an EtherType of 90-00 (not 0x9000, so they state it as an octet sequence, not a big-endian 16-bit value). It says of the two numerical fields in the protocol header:

> The skipCount and function code fields are 16 bit binary integers; the order of transmission is: least significant octet first, i.e. from the least significant bit to the most significant bit of the least significant octet.

so the only two fields it specifies as multi-octet numerical values are in *little*-endian byte order. (The "D" and "I"  of "DIX" were known at the time, to a large degree, for their lines of little-endian 8-bit-byte-addressable processors; the "X" was known for a couple of lines of 16-bit *word*-addressable processors.)

So, yeah, it really looks as if the whole notion of byte-swapping a MAC address is a Bluetooth invention; I'd *love* to hear their rationale for it. Unlike, say, EtherTypes, which, in practice, are often `#define`d and treated as 16-bit big-endian values in networking stacks, rather than as two-octet values, MAC addresses were generally processed as in-memory 6-octet values, and wouldn't be loaded into a register and processed (D and I, X's Alto) or pushed onto the evaluation stack (X's Mesa processors) and processed, they'd be copied and compared memory-to-memory, assembled an octet at a time from a human-readable string, and decoded an octet at a time to a human-readable string.

So I'd vote for `ENC_NORMAL` and `ENC_BYTE_SWAPPED` for `FT_ETHER` and `FT_EUI64`.

In a whole PFCP protocol is ENC_BIG_ENDIAN, and this ethertyp field refers to 2-octs from https://www.iana.org/assignments/ieee-802-numbers/ieee-802-numbers.xhtml#ieee-802-numbers-1

This however was never implemented :/ only showing a number, not the reflected value from the list
I couldn't find a value_string elsewhere in the codebase that has this..

I maybe should have made this draft.  Maybe the biggest question to answer is:

Do we care if ENC_NA is treated in many cases as a default (value is 0) that can stand in for ENC_BIG_ENDIAN (also 0), or do we want to insist that it is explicitly set?  README.dissector already says that it should be explicit.

In the case or packet-oran.c (part of this change), the protocol has an m-plane parameter that could set make of the multi-byte values to little endian.  Maybe that will never happen, but I would like to make it easier to add that preference by being explicit about those fields now.

If we agree to not use NA_ENC for integral values (apart from FT_[U]INT8 ?), I don't mind checking and changing the places that currently do it.

Added a check for FT_BOOLEAN, but only warn about it when field is > 8 bits.

> Do we care if ENC_NA is treated in many cases as a default (value is 0) that can stand in for ENC_BIG_ENDIAN (also 0), or do we want to insist that it is explicitly set? README.dissector already says that it should be explicit.

Not sure what you mean by "as a default"? I'd say that, for any field where the octet order is irrelevant (such as `FT_BYTES` and *maybe* `FT_INT8`/`FT_UINT8`), it should require that the encoding field be `ENC_NA` (and, given that those fields have no structure, probably no *other* `ENC_` values ORed in). For any field where it's relevant, `ENC_NA` should not be used.

For `FT_INT8`/`FT_UINT8`, 1) the byte order is irrelevant, as there's only one byte, but 2) it's numeric, and it may look cleaner if the encoding field matches that of multi-octet numeric fields.

(For `FT_CHAR`, the byte order is also irrelevant, but it might be useful to add `FT_CHAR4`, for ["char4"/"FourCC" values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FourCC) that are used in several places, and the byte order is relevant there, so maybe `FT_CHAR` should use the same encoding that `FT_INT8`/`FT_UINT8` would.)

By "as a default", I just meant that giving ENC_NA == ENC_BIG_ENDIAN == 0 is a lazy way to specify what is correct in most cases.  If the encoding value was at some point in the past a boolean type, maybe some nuance was lost in the conversion, or never existed.

The checks in the script are I think in agreement with what you said about FT_BYTES, FT_INT8 and FT_UINT8.  I didn't have anything for FT_CHAR, and I don't see any guidance in README.dissector, but a check shows that there are currently 31 calls with:
- ENC_NA (6)
- ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN (2)
- ENC_ASCII_7BITS (1)
- ENC_BIG_ENDIAN (4)
- ENC_ASCII (17)

I am noticing quite a few calls to proto_tree_add_item_ret_varint() using ENC_VARINT_QUIC -I'm not yet checking the 'encoding' value for all calls that include them, will work on that next

> By "as a default", I just meant that giving ENC_NA == ENC_BIG_ENDIAN == 0 is a lazy way to specify what is correct in most cases.

`ENC_NA` is the way to specify when there isn't a choice between "correct" and "incorrect". In particular, if, for one particular `FT_` type, there is one and only one encoding, `ENC_NA`, unlike `0`, indicate that the notion of the encoding to be used is "not applicable"; I consider it preferable to `0`, and to be a *correct* way to specify what's correct in cases where there is no "incorrect".

`ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` is the way to specify that this value is encoded the way it's represented in memory in a byte-addressed big-endian machine; th same applies to `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, *mutatis mutandis*. The *numerical values* of those two derives from pre-`ENC_` values for the API arguments now viewed as "encoding" arguments, from a time when the argument was a Boolean value meaning "is this little-endian?", and are chosen for binary compatibility for code still using `TRUE` and `FALSE`, if that's what you're alluding to when you say "If the encoding value was at some point in the past a boolean type, maybe some nuance was lost in the conversion, or never existed."

If there are no *other* `ENC_` values that would be used in the encoding argument, `ENC_NA` should be used. `ENC_NA` need not be used in cases where there's already an `ENC_` argument, such as `ENC_ASCII`, `ENC_ISO_8859_1`, `ENC_EBCDIC`, `ENC_MAC_ROMAN`, `ENC_UTF_8`, etc.. For *some* string encodings, such as `ENC_UTF_16`, you need `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` or `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN`.

> I didn't have anything for FT_CHAR, and I don't see any guidance in README.dissector, but a check shows that there are currently 31 calls with:
> 
> * ENC_NA (6)
> * ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN (2)
> * ENC_ASCII_7BITS (1)
> * ENC_BIG_ENDIAN (4)
> * ENC_ASCII (17)

The only one of those that is valid for a one-octet `FT_CHAR` is `ENC_ASCII`. If there are any *non*-ASCII single-character single-octet values ("non-ASCII" here including "extended ASCII, such as ISO 8859-1), those should be used *and* the code should be modified, if necessary, to handle those encodings.

For *non*-single-octet values, that presumably means it's either:

1. a one-character value in a non-single-octet fixed-width encoding such as UCS-2, in which case `ENC_UCS_2` should be used and the code should be modified, if necessary, to handle that;
2. a *multi*-character value, such as a FourCC, in a single-octet encoding, in which case there should be a new `FT_` encoding;
3. a one-character value in a *variable*-width encoding with no byte-order issue, such as UTF-8, in which case that should be supported *and* it should make sure that it's exactly one character (see 2) for multi-character values of that sort);
4. a one-character value in a variable-width encoding with a byte-order issue, such as UTF-16, in which case it's like 3), but with `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` or `ENC_LITTLE`ENDIAN.

@pquantin or @AndersBroman  - when you have time, could you please check the change to packet-nas_eps.c, which is to remove the ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN flags passed in for BCD strings?
@pquantin / @AndersBroman - could you please verify that BCD strings are still handled correctly in NAS-EPS with this change?

This change would switch how the BCD strings are handled in NAS-EPS.

As of commit 28902c6901888f57a84ba414d633e4461094dcc4 (pre 4.4.0), `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN / ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN` does have a meaning for `ENC_BCD_DIGITS_0_9`. That commit did not update the documentation, though.

The usual use in telephony protocols (and I think in NAS-EPS) is nibble-swapped, which that commit mapped to `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN`. A few protocols (zvt, mdb according to that commit) map the nibbles to the BCD digits in a perhaps more natural seeming order (high nibble to first digit, low nibble to second digit), which that commit mapped to `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN`.

This is perhaps a case where some slightly different terminology for the defines might be useful, in the same vein as to what @guyharris proposes above for `FT_ETHER`.

I reverted the changes to packet-nas_eps.c.  I'm not sure using the endian flags are right here either, as these refer to the order or bits within a byte, rather than the order of bytes within a multi-byte value?

Edit: I had this in draft but looks like I hadn't 'sent' it.

The telephony BCD value there is the order of digits/nibbles within a byte; it's possible to have a byte order that mixes one byte order for digit pairs within a number and another byte order for digits within a digit pair, e.g. "the most significant digit, and the digit after that, are in the first byte, but the *low*-order four bits of that byte are the most significant digit and the *high*-order four bits of that byte are the next most significant digit".

So maybe there should be separate `ENC_` values to specify the byte order and the digit order within the byte, e.g. add `ENC_NIBBLE_BIG_ENDIAN` and `ENC_NIBBLE_LITTLE_ENDIAN` (hopefully using "nibble" emphasizes that this is for nibbles *within* the byte?).

Does anyone object if I create issues to capture some of the discussions that have happened here, and merge this change as it is tomorrow sometime?

./tools/check_typed_item_calls.py currently emits 1994 warnings about encoding values.  I would be more comfortable dealing with them in manageable batches as I refine the checks that the script does, then if/when if doesn't find anything, we can decide whether some/all of them should be errors?

> Does anyone object if I create issues to capture some of the discussions that have happened here, and merge this change as it is tomorrow sometime?

I don't mind; presumably the changes that need further discussion won't be in that commit.

Part of the problem here is that the encoding is a combination of several components, with the components and their possible values differing by type:

Fixed-length integers:

* only one "base" encoding, 2's complement binary
* at least for lengths > 1 octet, the byte order

Variable-length integers:

* "base" encodings Protobuf varint, QUIC, Protobuf zig-zag, SDNV
* byte order for any of those?

Floating-point numbers:

* currently, the only "base" encoding is IEEE binary - I guess we could do the two VAX encodings, IBM hexadecimal, and IEEE decimal, but I'm not sure the need has popped up
* byte order

Strings:

* a bunch of encodings, including TBCD - should TBCD be a separate `FT_` type?
* byte order for UTF-16, UCS-2, and UCS-4
* order of digits *within* the octet for TBCD
* length encoding for counted strings, either normal 2's complement or Zigbee
* "string gets its byte order from a BOM" for UTF-16, UCS-2, and UCS-4

Byte arrays:

* encoding is either raw octet values or a text string of hex digits
* for the latter, the separator used between hex digit pairs

Absolute times:

* various formats/epochs, plus "string"
* for string, the format of the string

Relative times:

* various formats

We probably don't want an encoding value of 0, as that doesn't directly give any information.

For any encoding for which the byte order matters, we should *require* that one of `ENC_BIG_ENDIAN` or `ENC_LITTLE_ENDIAN` be specified - don't allow "defaulting" to big-endian. That ensures there's at least one `ENC_` value.

For single-octet numbers, we could require choosing an endianness based on whatever  endianness is used for other values, or we could allow `ENC_NA` to make sure there' *something* there.

For strings, we should require one of the string encoding values. Byte order - big-endian, little-endian, and "see the BOM" if supported - is only necessary for multi-byte encodings that support both byte orders.

For byte arrays, allow `ENC_NA` for raw octets.

Times require an encoding - there's no default.

Thanks for the good summary, Guy.  Will merge current state - should not report any false positives (will only warn if flags appeared that should never be there), and morph it into more detailed checks you described above.
